title: Distinct Even Numbers From Three Digit Cards
statement:
You have a pile of digit cards, given as the array digits. Pick three different cards and lay them in a row to form a three-digit number. The number must be even and must not start with 0.

Return how many distinct numbers you can form. Two cards showing the same digit can both be used, but the same card cannot be used twice, and a number formed in several ways counts once.

examples.why: Ending in 2, the first two places take any ordered pair from {1, 3, 4}: 6 numbers. Ending in 4: another 6.
220 and 202. 022 starts with 0, and the two 2 cards make the same numbers either way, so duplicates count once.
No even digit to put last.

hints: Choosing cards and removing duplicate results is messy. Flip it around: how many three-digit even numbers exist at all?
There are only 450 even numbers from 100 to 998. For each one, can it be built from the cards?
Count how many cards show each digit. A number is buildable when, for every digit, it uses that digit no more times than there are cards for it.

explain.intuition:
The direct way picks three different card positions, builds the number, and puts it in a set to remove duplicates. With at most 10 cards that is only 720 ordered triples, so it is perfectly fine.

The cleaner idea flips the question. Instead of building numbers from cards, check each candidate number against the cards. There are only 450 even numbers from 100 to 998. Count the cards per digit; a candidate is buildable if each of its three digits is used no more often than its card count. Duplicates and leading zeros disappear on their own: each candidate is counted once, and none starts with 0.
steps: Count how many cards show each digit 0–9.
For each even x from 100 to 998, split it into its three digits.
Count how often each digit appears in x; if every digit fits within its card count, add 1.
pitfalls: Counting ordered triples of cards instead of distinct numbers. Two cards with the same digit produce the same numbers.
Allowing a leading zero, so 022 sneaks in as a three-digit number.
Checking only that each digit exists among the cards, so 666 is accepted from a single 6 card.

solutions.title: All ordered triples in a set
solutions.idea: Try every choice of three different card positions, keep valid even numbers in a set.

solutions.title: Check every candidate against card counts
solutions.idea: Test each even number from 100 to 998: does it use any digit more often than there are cards for it?

followups: Return the numbers themselves in increasing order. Which version gives them sorted for free?
Build k-digit numbers divisible by 3 instead. Does checking every candidate still scale?
